source: El Lahib et al. (2026) Temporal leakage in search-engine date-filtered web retrieval
finding: Date-filtered web search leaks post-cutoff facts. With leaked sources an LLM looks far better; with leak-free sources it is no better than no retrieval.
numbers: 393 Google / 389 DuckDuckGo Metaculus questions; 38,879 / 34,454 URLs; 33.2% / 34.5% of URLs carry post-cutoff info. 41.0% / 54.8% of questions have a direct-answer page. gpt-oss-120b on 93 binary 2025 questions: no retrieval Brier 0.244; leak-free (score 0) 0.242; scores 2-4 0.128; scores 3-4 0.108; score 4 only 0.129. Judge vs 2 humans on 134 docs: 76.1% exact, QWK 0.85.
limits: Same model is leakage judge and forecaster. Only Google, DDG, Metaculus. Mitigations (Wayback, snapshots) not tested. The 0.108 vs 0.242 contrast is leaky vs leak-free retrieval inside the retrospective setup, not retrospective vs live.
agent_relevance: Retrieval gains reported on retrospective questions may be mostly leakage. Our agent must score only post-cutoff or live questions; leak-free retrieval gave about zero gain here.

source: Li, Wang, El Lahib, Xia, Pi (2026) Simulated Ignorance Fails
finding: Telling a model to forget post-cutoff knowledge does not work. Models do much better on pre-cutoff (retrospective) questions than on post-cutoff ones, and humans show no such gap.
numbers: 9 models (6 non-reasoning, 3 reasoning), about 470-477 binary questions (about 201 pre-cutoff, 273-276 post). Mean Brier about 0.11 pre/SI vs 0.24 post/TI (gap about 0.13; one figure says 0.26 TI). Cutoff instruction closes 48% of the gap. Reasoning models gaps 0.086 and 0.097 vs 0.064 and 0.067 for non-reasoning. Humans 0.232 pre vs 0.243 post. Gap largest for geopolitics (0.111), smallest for business (0.010). Each pair run 3 times.
limits: Paper is internally inconsistent on TI Brier (0.24 vs 0.26) and question count (470 vs 477). Question mix differs pre vs post.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models leak more, not less. Any forecasting gain measured on pre-cutoff questions should be discounted heavily. Halawi used a post-cutoff test set, so this hits later reproductions more.

source: De-Arteaga, Dubrawski, Chouldechova (2018) Learning under selective labels in the presence of expert consistency
finding: Models trained only on cases a human chose to label learn 'what happens when a human predicts risk', not the true risk. Methods that assume every case could have been labelled fail when humans are consistent.
numbers: Child-welfare data: 83,311 referrals, 47,305 children, 2010-2014, 800+ variables; random forest, 75/25 split. Semi-synthetic test: what is learned from observed labels does not generalise to cases humans confidently screen out.
limits: Applies to the selective-labels setting generally; critiques contraction-type methods used by Kleinberg/Lakkaraju. Not a direct rebuttal of the QJE bail estimate.
agent_relevance: Whenever the agent only sees outcomes of its own past choices, its fitted formula is biased. Log counterfactual outcomes or keep an exploration slice.

source: Kleinberg, Lakkaraju, Leskovec, Ludwig, Mullainathan (2017/18) Human decisions and machine predictions (NBER w23180), caveats
finding: The authors themselves flag the assumptions behind the bail result: selection on observables, selective labels and omitted payoffs. They say earlier clinical-vs-statistical work suffered from the same issues.
numbers: Headline: at judges' own release rate the algorithm gives 24.7% fewer crimes; at the same crime rate it jails 41.8% fewer. Stricter judges: +13.0 pp jailing for -18.7% crime vs lenient quintile; detaining by risk would need only +6.3 pp. Predicted-judge rule beats actual judges 'by a wide margin'.
quote: The unobservables create noise, not signal.
limits: Quasi-random judge assignment is the main defence; a bounding exercise (Table 5) shows results shrink under extreme assumptions. NYC data plus national replication. The soft-information claim is an inference, not a direct test.
agent_relevance: The Meehl-style edge is robust here, but only with a quasi-random check. For our agent, hold-out checks must use cases whose labels were not chosen by the agent.

source: Kleinberg et al. (2018) judge-leniency test of unobservables
finding: Test of the rebuttal that lenient judges use soft information: train the algorithm on lenient judges' released cases and impute outcomes for strict judges' released cases. Imputed and actual crime match on average, so no sign lenient judges are unusually good with unobservables.
numbers: Imputed vs actual crime described as 'quite similar on average' for each stricter-judge quintile; a second test uses intra-judge variation. No p-value read.
limits: Limited power against a small soft-information effect. Relies on random assignment of cases to judges.
agent_relevance: Soft information can be tested: compare formula vs holistic only where the holistic path had extra information. For LLM agents the soft info is whatever is not in the feature list.

source: Norman, Rivera, Hughes (2026) Reliability without Validity: large-scale LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
finding: Judge LLMs can be very repeatable and still biased. Test-retest above 0.95 coexists with position bias above 0.10. Raw agreement overstates skill.
numbers: 21 judges, nine providers, three benchmarks, 118 runs, about 541,000 judgments. Kappa deflation vs exact match 33-41 pp on MT-Bench. Rankings shift by up to 14 positions across benchmarks. Position bias from 0.002 (Gemini 2.5 Pro) to above 0.10 in two production judges.
limits: Pairwise preference judging, not 0-10 feature scores. Says nothing about averaging k samples.
agent_relevance: Repeatability of a feature rating is not evidence it is right. Averaging k samples removes sampling noise only, not a fixed bias. Randomise order and check validity separately.

source: Huynh, Gomez, Deviyani, Shelby, Bigham, Diaz (2026) Quantifying the statistical effect of rubric modifications on human-autorater agreement
finding: Closest found test of 'LLM scores parts, code combines' vs 'LLM scores whole'. Decomposed (analytic) rubrics did not beat holistic ones in instruction following; the aggregation rule mattered.
numbers: GPT-4o and Llama-3.1-70B. Instruction following, GPT-4o Kendall tau vs humans: holistic zero-shot 0.536, holistic 3-shot 0.585, analytic separate calls 0.464, analytic batch 0.167, analytic edited 0.471. Llama holistic 0.470/0.578, batch analytic 0.166. Essays: holistic beat most analytic prompts for prompts 4 and 6; prompt 1 favoured analytic. Examples and context raised agreement; complexity and conservative aggregation (Pareto) lowered it.
limits: Target is agreement with human raters on grading, not accuracy on a reasoning task. Aggregation was ratio-of-yes or Pareto, not a weighted or fitted formula. Batch analytic had yes-bias. Last 8k characters of page unread.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that decomposition beats holistic for an LLM at equal tokens. A naive code formula (ratio of yes) can lose. Test per task.

source: Salganik et al. (2020) Measuring the predictability of life outcomes with a scientific mass collaboration (PNAS 117:8398)
finding: In a low-ceiling domain even the best of 160 teams barely beat a 4-variable benchmark.
numbers: 457 applications, 160 valid teams, six outcomes, thousands of predictors. Best holdout R2 about 0.2 for material hardship and GPA, about 0.05 for grit, eviction, layoff, job training. Baseline: 4-variable linear/logistic model (mother's race, marital status, education at birth, plus outcome or proxy at age 9); it outperformed many submissions. Submissions were more like each other than like the truth, so ensembling gave little.
limits: One dataset and six outcomes. Best-of-160 on same holdout is slightly optimistic. Exact per-outcome values only in a figure.
agent_relevance: The agent should compare to a base rate or tiny benchmark and report 'little better than baseline' when the gap is small. More models or samples will not help if errors are shared.

source: Satopaa, Pemantle, Ungar (2014) Modeling probability forecasts via information diversity
finding: Optimal extremizing depends on how much forecasters' information overlaps. The factor can be derived from the forecasts themselves, with no outcomes needed.
numbers: GJP super-forecasters year 2: 44 forecasters, 123 binary events, 17-34 forecasts per event (mean 24.2), first-three-days forecast. Mean Brier: simple average 0.132, log pool 0.128, probit pool 0.128, revealed aggregator 0.123; base rate 0.187.
limits: One group (supers), one year. Gain 0.132 to 0.123 (about 7%). Authors call it a first attempt. Needs many forecasters per question.
agent_relevance: With k LLM samples you could set extremization from their disagreement with no resolved questions. Samples from one model overlap heavily, so the safe factor is probably smaller than for humans (untested).

source: Neyman & Roughgarden (2022) Are you smarter than a random expert? The robust aggregation of substitutable signals
finding: Worst-case argument for averaging then extremizing by a constant factor, under 'projective substitutes'. Only the abstract page was read; the sqrt(3) value is not on that page.
numbers: Abstract only; constant not read here.
limits: Abstract page only, so the sqrt(3) derivation was not checked. A forum comment (search snippet, unopened) claims it matched an optimised constant on 899 Metaculus questions.
agent_relevance: The sqrt(3) factor is a worst-case choice under a substitutes assumption with many forecasters. Its fit to LLM ensembles is unproven.

source: Angelova, Dobbie, Yang (2023) Algorithmic recommendations and human discretion (NBER w31747)
finding: Overrides of an algorithm by bail judges mostly hurt. A small group beat the algorithm when they used private information and avoided over-reacting to salient events.
numbers: About 90% of judges did worse than the algorithm when they overrode it. Most override decisions were about as accurate as random guessing. About 10% of judges beat the algorithm on accuracy and fairness.
limits: Abstract page only; exact sample and effect sizes not read. Bail setting only.
agent_relevance: Broken-leg rule: allow the holistic verdict to override the formula only on a flagged, nameable reason, and log it. Default to the formula.

source: AIA Forecaster technical report (2025): fixed sqrt(3) extremization and ensemble size
finding: AIA used d = sqrt(3) from Neyman and Roughgarden, not fit on its data, 'to avoid overfitting'. The gain is small. Its own fitted optimum was higher.
numbers: FB-7-21, 498 questions: no correction Brier 0.1140; fixed Platt 0.1076 (-0.0064); fixed log-odds extremization 0.1085; leave-one-out learned 0.1071; fit on Halawi benchmark and tested out of distribution 0.1104. Superforecaster-optimal coefficient 1.72; AIA learned optimum 2.27 (not used). 10 forecasts per question; single 0.1182, mean of 10 0.1140, median 0.1138, trimmed 0.1142. Drop steep from 1 to 5 forecasts, small after.
limits: Question count for the out-of-distribution fit not stated. Appendices A and E and the last 40k characters unread.
agent_relevance: A fixed prior factor plus about 5-10 samples captures most of the gain. A fit on one benchmark tested on another still gave 0.1104 vs 0.1140 uncorrected, so the fit transfers somewhat. No question-count curve found.

source: AIA Forecaster technical report (2025): leakage controls and results
finding: AIA filtered leaked search results with an LLM judge and blocked market domains, then checked robustness. Results stay near superforecasters but not clearly above them.
numbers: Leak-judge audit n=502: 16 TP, 65 FP, 412 TN, 9 FN. About 1.65% of results had foreknowledge bias. Dropping flagged questions: 0.1159 to 0.1161. Brier AIA vs supers: FB-7-21 (498) 0.1076 vs 0.1110; FB-8-14 (602) 0.1099 vs 0.1152; FB-Market (76) 0.0753 vs 0.0740 (market 0.0965); MarketLiquid (1610) 0.1258, market 0.1106 (market better). Live closed markets n=64: with search 0.1002, without 0.3609, market 0.1111.
limits: Filter flags are noisy (16 of 81 flags true). Live closed-market n is small. Authors say 'statistically indistinguishable' from supers; intervals not read.
agent_relevance: Leak filtering plus live evaluation survives better than raw retrospective numbers, but the edge over supers is within noise. Search matters a lot live (0.10 vs 0.36).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting: ablation section (re-read)
finding: Corrects the doubtful ablation value. 0.186 is the full system with retrieval but no fine-tuning of the reasoning model, not 'base GPT-4 only'. No fine-tuning and no retrieval scores 0.206, close to the best zero-shot baseline of 0.208.
numbers: Full system 0.179. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 swapped in: 0.182. No fine-tuning: 0.186 (+0.007). No fine-tuning and no retrieval: 0.206. Best zero-shot baseline 0.208. Dataset 3,762 questions across 5 platforms.
limits: Test set is post-cutoff by design; leakage issues in d01/d02 apply to later reproductions that use search engines.
agent_relevance: Most of the gain is retrieval (0.206 to 0.186); fine-tuning adds about 0.007; prompt search adds little.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) calibration and ensembling findings
finding: The system was already well calibrated, and binning or isotonic regression did not help. Trimmed mean beat mean, median, geometric mean and USC.
numbers: Zero-shot base models were less calibrated. Trimmed mean best on validation among 5 ensemble methods.
quote: standard calibration methods such as binning or isotonic regression do not improve performance
limits: Does not test Platt or extremization; ensemble of 6 forecasts. Claim is in text, no table read.
agent_relevance: Do not assume recalibration helps: check on a held-out slice first. Trimmed mean is a safe default.
